questions.prompt: In an overloaded function, which signatures can callers use?

options.text: The implementation signature
Only the overload signatures; the implementation signature isn't callable from outside
All signatures equally
None — overloads are documentation only

questions.explanation: Callers see only the overload signatures. The implementation signature exists to satisfy them and isn't part of the public callable type.

questions.prompt: What does a `this` parameter do, and does it affect the arguments?

options.text: It adds a required first argument callers must pass
It types the value of `this` inside the function; it's type-only, erased, and doesn't change the real parameters
It makes the function static
It binds this permanently at runtime

questions.explanation: A this parameter is a type-only first parameter. It types this and is erased; callers don't pass it and the real arguments are unchanged.

questions.prompt: How is an assertion function different from a type guard?

options.text: There is no difference
A type guard returns a boolean you branch on; an assertion function throws on failure and narrows the value for the rest of the scope
An assertion function returns a boolean; a type guard throws
Assertion functions only work on numbers

questions.explanation: A type guard returns a boolean predicate. An assertion function throws if the condition fails and, via an asserts return type, narrows without an if.

questions.prompt: Write the return annotation that narrows `value` to string if the function doesn't throw: asserts value ______ string. (one word)
questions.explanation: `asserts value is string` narrows value to string for the rest of the scope when the assertion function returns.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer a single signature over overloads?

options.text: Never — overloads are always better
When a union return type is just as accurate — overloads add complexity and can hide mistakes
Only when there is one parameter
Only in non-strict mode

questions.explanation: Overloads are worthwhile only when the return type genuinely depends on the argument shape; otherwise a single signature is clearer and safer.

questions.prompt: What happens if an assertion function's runtime check doesn't match its `asserts` type?

options.text: The compiler catches it automatically
The compiler still trusts the assertion, producing an unsafe narrowing that can crash at runtime
It becomes a syntax error
Nothing — assertions have no effect

questions.explanation: As with type guards, the compiler trusts the assertion. A dishonest runtime check yields an unsafe narrowing and possible runtime errors.
